intent: 30 candidates: 20 new and 10 second attempts at batch-2 dishes that were refused once. Fifteen of the thirty are Egyptian — half the pool — because the catalogue is 26.4% Egyptian against a ≥30% goal, and none of them is a foreign dish wearing an Egyptian name to move the number. The weighting is to real meals: a baked tilapia, white beans with beef, a tray of torly, chicken livers, two breakfasts built on cheese and eggs. The nine dishes refused twice in batches 1 and 2 are NOT here — they are retired from automated attempts and kept in the backlog for a human with a known-good source. Belila, gibna-bel-tamatem and sogo2-bel-salsa found nothing twice and are deferred.

candidates.name: Baked Tilapia with Cumin
candidates.note: Bolti is the fish Egypt actually eats and the catalogue has no baked whole fish. Five lines and an oven.

candidates.name: Baked Mixed Vegetables in Tomato
candidates.note: One tray, whatever vegetables are in the house, tomato over the top. The cheapest way to feed a family in this catalogue if it lands.

candidates.name: White Beans with Beef
candidates.note: The Sunday pot. Distinct from the vegetarian tomato-and-white-bean stew already in the catalogue: this one is built on beef and stock.

candidates.name: Chicken Livers with Onion
candidates.note: Cheaper and softer than the Alexandrian beef liver, and a different dish. The chicken-liver row is used by nothing.

candidates.name: Eggs with White Cheese
candidates.note: Four lines. Breakfast is still the thinnest meal type in the catalogue.

candidates.name: Areesh Cheese with Oil and Tomato
candidates.note: The cheapest protein on an Egyptian breakfast table and the areesh row is used by nothing at all.

candidates.name: Dried Fruit Compote
candidates.note: Soaked overnight, eaten at iftar. Five lines, no cooking, and it uses three dried-fruit rows that no recipe touches.

candidates.name: Stuffed Ramadan Pancakes
candidates.note: The Ramadan sweet. Six lines; the batter is flour, semolina and yeast and the filling is nuts.

candidates.name: Tamarind Drink
candidates.note: Three lines, and the tamarind row exists for exactly this and is used by nothing.

candidates.name: Bread Pudding in Syrup
candidates.note: Stale bread, syrup and cream. A real Egyptian dessert built out of what is going hard in the bread bin.

candidates.name: Cheese Börek
candidates.note: Four lines from bought phyllo. Turkey's version of the same idea as sambousek and a different shape on the plate.

candidates.name: Chilled Tomato Soup
candidates.note: No cooking at all, served cold, which matters somewhere that is 38°C in August.

candidates.name: Greek Egg and Lemon Soup
candidates.note: Rice, egg and lemon whisked into a broth. Cheap, restorative, and nothing like it in the catalogue.

candidates.name: Lentil and Chickpea Soup
candidates.note: The Moroccan Ramadan soup. Legumes are the catalogue's joint-largest protein group and this is a substantial one.

candidates.name: Lemon and Oregano Roast Potatoes
candidates.note: Roasted in lemon and stock until the edges catch. Six lines, one tray.

candidates.name: Onion Soup with Cheese Toast
candidates.note: A kilo of onions and almost nothing else. Made here with roumy on baladi bread, which is what an Egyptian kitchen has.

candidates.name: Tomato and Bread Salad
candidates.note: The other stale-bread dish, and the summer counterpart to fattoush.

candidates.name: Potato-Stuffed Flatbread
candidates.note: Six pantry lines and a dry pan. Filling, cheap, and no oven needed.

candidates.name: Eggs in Spiced Tomato
candidates.note: Boiled eggs simmered in tomato. A main built on the cheapest protein there is.

candidates.name: Beans in Tomato Molasses
candidates.note: Five lines and it keeps for days. The molasses row is Egyptian black honey and is used by almost nothing.

candidates.name: Salted Rice Parcels
candidates.note: Three lines. Cold lunch, travels well, and it uses the nori row that nothing else does.

candidates.name: Spiced Bean Soup
candidates.note: A tin of beans into a blender. Six lines, one pot, under half an hour.

candidates.name: Macaroni in Red Sauce
candidates.note: SECOND ATTEMPT. The first candidate was a pasta alla norma with aubergine and cheese in it. Probably the most-cooked weeknight dinner in Egypt, so it is worth one more try.

candidates.name: Eggs Scrambled with Tomato
candidates.note: SECOND ATTEMPT. The first candidate was a hotel buffet chafing dish with its label showing.

candidates.name: Cheese Sambousek
candidates.note: SECOND ATTEMPT. The first candidate was Indian samosas with a green potato filling.

candidates.name: Fried Aubergine with Garlic and Vinegar
candidates.note: SECOND ATTEMPT. The first candidate was Spanish berenjenas con miel — battered and drizzled with honey.

candidates.name: Whole Chicken in the Oven with Cumin
candidates.note: SECOND ATTEMPT. The first candidate was a painted restaurant sign reading BROILER-BAR. The whole-chicken row still has no recipe.

candidates.name: Yogurt Flatbread
candidates.note: SECOND ATTEMPT. The first candidate was a restaurant buffet line with a basket of naan in the corner.

candidates.name: Cabbage and Carrot Slaw
candidates.note: SECOND ATTEMPT. The first candidate was a diner plate of corn dogs with a ramekin of slaw at the edge.

candidates.name: Crumbed Chicken Cutlet
candidates.note: SECOND ATTEMPT. The first candidate was katsu CURRY — the sauce was most of the plate. This is بانيه, one of the most ordered things in Egypt, and the catalogue has no crumbed cutlet.
